\chapter{And, and Also}
\label{ch:ta-and-and-also}
\hlchaptermodality{74}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can join two things with -um, say that one more thing applies too, and deny both at once.}

Complete TA-C74-neither and say a two-item list, then the same list denied.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[-um … -um]{-\ta{உம்} … -\ta{உம்} — how Tamil says \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C74-and}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mādam} mean, and what did \emph{āṇḍu} mean?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: no word goes between them}]
\textbf{-\ta{உம்} … -\ta{உம்}} (\emph{-um … -um}) — \textquotedblleft{}both … and\textquotedblright{}.

English drops a word \emph{between} two things. Tamil puts an ending on \textbf{each} of them and leaves the space between them empty.

\ta{பால்} (\emph{pāl}) is milk. \ta{தேநீர்} (\emph{tēnīr}) is tea. Milk and tea:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{பாலும்} \ta{தேநீரும்}} — \emph{pālum tēnīrum}
\end{quote}

Both words are still there, in the same order, and nothing new sits between them. Each one has grown a tail instead.

The tail is always \textbf{-\ta{உம்}}, and it lands on every item in the list — the last one included. Two things, two tails.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you have} & \textbf{you say} \\
\midrule
\ta{பால்}, \ta{தேநீர்} & \textbf{\ta{பாலும்} \ta{தேநீரும்}} \\
\ta{மேசை}, \ta{கட்டில்} & \textbf{\ta{மேசையும்} \ta{கட்டிலும்}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\ta{மேசை} ends in a vowel, so a light \textbf{\ta{ய்}} slides in before the ending: \ta{மேசை}\textbf{\ta{யும்}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first thing so far that joins two words you already had.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pālum tēnīrum}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mēsaiyum kaṭṭilum}
  \item \emph{Count:} how many tails a list of two carries
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mādam}, then say \emph{āṇḍu}, then join the two — \emph{mādamum āṇḍum}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{nēṟṟu}, \emph{kuṭai} and \emph{tarai} — three distances back — then join two of them with -\ta{உம்}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does Tamil keep its \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{On the end of every item, as -\ta{உம்} — never between them.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-um]{-\ta{உம்} on its own — \textquotedblleft{}also\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}too\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C74-also}



\begin{quote}
Say milk and tea in Tamil. How many \textbf{-\ta{உம்}} endings did that take?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: one tail, not two}]
Put \textbf{-\ta{உம்}} on two words and you have joined them. Put it on \textbf{one} word and it means something else: \emph{that one too}.

\ta{நான்} (\emph{nāṉ}) is \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}. \ta{நான்} with the tail:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{நானும்}} — \emph{nāṉum} — \textquotedblleft{}me too\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Somebody says they are going. You say \textbf{\ta{நானும்}} and you are going with them. One word, one ending, a whole reply.

The same tail on the things around you:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{with -\ta{உம்}} & \textbf{it means} \\
\midrule
\ta{நீங்கள்} & \textbf{\ta{நீங்களும்}} & you too \\
\ta{இது} & \textbf{\ta{இதுவும்}} & this one too \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\ta{இது} ends in a vowel, so \textbf{\ta{வ்}} slides in the way \textbf{\ta{ய்}} did after \ta{மேசை}.

This is one of the most-used endings in the language, and you have now met both of its jobs.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One ending, two jobs: on two words it joins, on one word it adds.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nāṉum}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nīṅgaḷum}, then \emph{iduvum}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{pālum tēnīrum} against \emph{pālum} alone — two tails join, one tail adds
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{āṇḍu}, then say \emph{pālum tēnīrum}, then say \emph{nāṉum}
  \item \emph{Return to:} read \textbf{\ta{இன்று}}, say \emph{tuṭaippam} and say \emph{kūrai} — three distances back — then join two of them with -\ta{உம்}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Someone says they are leaving and you are leaving too. One word. (\textbf{\ta{நானும்}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pālum]{\ta{பாலும்} — an ending you can now see}

\label{lesson:TA-W29-read-paalum}



\begin{quote}
Before the page: say \emph{pālum tēnīrum}, then say \emph{nāṉum}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{பாலும்} — where the tail begins}
You have read \textbf{\ta{பால்}} already. Adding the joining ending changes one thing on the page, and it is worth seeing exactly where.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{பா}} & \emph{pā} & \ta{ப} with the long-\textbf{\ta{ா}} sign \\
\textbf{\ta{லு}} & \emph{lu} & \ta{ல} with the \textbf{\ta{ு}} sign \\
\textbf{\ta{ம்}} & \emph{m} & \ta{ம} with a \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{பா} · \ta{லு} · \ta{ம்} $\to$ \ta{பாலும்}}
\end{quote}

Look at what happened to the middle. In \textbf{\ta{பால்}} the \ta{ல} carried a \ta{புள்ளி} and had no vowel of its own. The ending brings a \textbf{\ta{உ}}, the \ta{ல} takes it, and the \ta{புள்ளி} moves along to the \ta{ம்} that arrived with it.

Nothing was inserted between two words. The seam is inside the word.

The same seam in \textbf{\ta{தேநீரும்}}: \ta{ர} picks up \textbf{\ta{ு}}, and \ta{ம்} closes the word.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{பா}} — then \textbf{\ta{லு}} — then \textbf{\ta{ம்}}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{பாலும்} \ta{தேநீரும்}}
  \item \emph{Point to:} the letter that lost its \ta{புள்ளி}, and say where the \ta{புள்ளி} went
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pālum tēnīrum}, then say \emph{nāṉum}, then read \textbf{\ta{பாலும்}}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{muṉbu}, \emph{sīppu} and \emph{eḻu} — three distances back — then join two of them with -\ta{உம்}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{பாலும்}}. Which letter changed when the ending arrived? (\textbf{\ta{ல} — it took the \ta{உ} the ending brought.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-um … -um illai]{-\ta{உம்} … -\ta{உம்} \ta{இல்லை} — neither one nor the other}

\label{lesson:TA-C74-neither}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{nāṉum}. Then read \textbf{\ta{பாலும்}} aloud.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: the list stays, the end changes}]
English swaps the whole join to say the opposite: \emph{both … and} becomes \emph{neither … nor}. Tamil keeps the join it already has and puts \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} after it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{பாலும்} \ta{தேநீரும்} \ta{இல்லை}} — \emph{pālum tēnīrum illai} — \textquotedblleft{}neither milk nor tea\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\ta{இல்லை} is the very first word of chapter one, the one that means \emph{no, there isn't}. It has been waiting for a list to stand at the end of.

Say the shop has neither:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you say} & \textbf{it means} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{பாலும்} \ta{தேநீரும்}} & milk and tea \\
\textbf{\ta{பாலும்} \ta{தேநீரும்} \ta{இல்லை}} & neither milk nor tea \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One word longer, and the meaning has turned over. Nothing inside the list moved.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four things in this chapter and only one ending: joining, adding, reading the seam, denying the lot.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pālum tēnīrum illai}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mēsaiyum kaṭṭilum illai}
  \item \emph{Turn:} say the list, then say it again with \ta{இல்லை} on the end
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nāṉum}, then read \textbf{\ta{பாலும்}}, then say \emph{pālum tēnīrum illai}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{mādam}, \emph{pasi} and \emph{tūṅgu} — three distances back — then join two of them with -\ta{உம்}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The shop has neither milk nor tea. Say it. (\textbf{\ta{பாலும்} \ta{தேநீரும்} \ta{இல்லை}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
